CIA triad
Which part of the CIA triad does ransomware that encrypts a hospital's records attack most directly?
Availability
Confidentiality only
Non-repudiation
Authentication
Encrypting data so it cannot be used denies access, which is an attack on availability. Modern ransomware often also steals data, adding a confidentiality impact.
m
CIA triad
An attacker changes the amount on an invoice in a database without being noticed. Which property is violated?
Integrity
Availability
Confidentiality
Accountability
Integrity means data is accurate and has not been altered without authorisation.
d
CIA trade-offs
Why can strengthening confidentiality sometimes reduce availability?
Stricter controls such as encryption and MFA can block or slow legitimate access
Confidentiality controls always delete data that has not been used recently
Encrypted data cannot be backed up, so outages last longer
Confidentiality and availability are measured by the same metric
Security properties trade off. Lost keys or strict lockouts can stop authorised users from reaching data.
m
Kill chain
In the Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain, which phase comes first?
Reconnaissance
Delivery
Exploitation
Installation
The phases are reconnaissance, weaponisation, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, and actions on objectives.
d
Kill chain
Why does the Kill Chain encourage defenders to act early in an intrusion?
Breaking any earlier link stops the attack before its objective
Later phases cannot be detected by any security tool
Attackers abandon campaigns after the reconnaissance phase
Early phases are the only ones covered by law
Disrupting delivery or exploitation prevents the later phases, which is cheaper than responding to a completed breach.
m
Kill chain
A phishing email carrying a malicious attachment reaches a user's inbox. Which Kill Chain phase is this?
Delivery
Reconnaissance
Weaponisation
Actions on objectives
Delivery is the transmission of the weapon to the target, such as by email, web or USB.
d
Attacker economics
Why is it often said that defenders must be right every time while attackers need to be right once?
Defenders must cover the whole attack surface; one gap may be enough
Attackers are legally allowed one free attempt per organisation
Defenders are rated on a pass/fail exam held each year
Attackers cannot repeat an attack after a first failure
The asymmetry reflects broad defensive coverage versus a single successful path. Layered defence and detection reduce the impact of any one gap.
m
Incident history
What did the 1988 Morris worm demonstrate?
Self-replicating code could disrupt a large part of the early internet
Email attachments could be used to deliver ransomware
Nation-states could damage industrial equipment with malware
Cloud services could be taken over through weak passwords
The Morris worm spread across thousands of internet-connected Unix systems, and led to the creation of the first CERT.
d
Incident history
What made Stuxnet (discovered in 2010) a landmark incident?
It caused physical damage to industrial equipment through malicious code
It was the first malware ever to spread by email attachment
It stole the largest number of credit card numbers of its time
It encrypted files and demanded payment in cryptocurrency
Stuxnet targeted industrial control systems driving centrifuges, showing that cyber attacks can have physical effects.
m
Incident history
Which weakness was exploited in the 2017 WannaCry outbreak?
An SMBv1 vulnerability patched by Microsoft earlier that year (MS17-010)
A weak default password on internet-connected webcams
A flaw in the TLS protocol used by online banking sites
A malicious update pushed through a software vendor's build system
WannaCry spread through the EternalBlue exploit for MS17-010, which had been patched about two months earlier. Unpatched systems were hit.
d
Incident history
What is the main lesson of the 2017 Equifax breach for vulnerability management?
A known, patchable flaw left unpatched can lead to a massive breach
Encryption of data at rest prevents all breaches of web applications
Breaches only happen to organisations without any security team
Cloud migration is the main cause of large data breaches
Attackers exploited an Apache Struts vulnerability for which a patch was available. Asset inventory and timely patching matter.
d
Incident history
What made the SolarWinds compromise (disclosed 2020) especially dangerous?
Malicious code was inserted into a trusted vendor's software update
It used a password-guessing attack against internet-facing email servers
It spread through infected USB drives inside government offices
It exploited a bug in the TCP/IP stack of every operating system
Supply chain attacks abuse trust in signed vendor updates, reaching many customers at once.
m
Assets
In information security, what is an asset?
Anything of value to the organisation that needs protection
Only the computers and servers listed in the IT budget
A vulnerability that an attacker can exploit
A security tool purchased to protect the network
Assets include data, hardware, software, people, services and reputation.
m
Data states
Which data state does full-disk encryption protect?
Data at rest
Data in transit
Data in use
Data in motion over Wi-Fi
Disk encryption protects stored data. TLS protects data in transit; protecting data in use needs other controls.
d
Data states
Why is data in use the hardest state to protect?
It must be decrypted in memory for processing
It is always stored on removable media
It is never covered by any access control
It is transmitted without any network protocol
Processing usually needs plaintext in memory; technologies such as confidential computing aim to reduce that exposure.
m
Asset inventory
Why does a security programme start with an asset inventory?
You cannot protect what you do not know you have
Inventories are required before any antivirus can be installed
Attackers cannot target assets that appear in an inventory
Insurance companies refuse to insure unlisted laptops
Unknown assets are unpatched and unmonitored. The inventory drives classification, risk assessment and controls.
d
Asset classification
Why should assets be classified by value and sensitivity?
To focus the strongest protection on what matters most
Because every asset must receive identical controls
So that low-value assets can be removed from monitoring
Because classification replaces the need for encryption
Classification lets limited resources be prioritised according to impact.
m
Attack surface
What is an organisation's attack surface?
The total set of points where an attacker could try to get in or extract data
The number of firewalls deployed at the network perimeter
The physical area of the data centre floor
The list of attackers who have targeted the organisation
The attack surface spans digital, physical and human entry points.
m
Attack surface
Which is an example of the human attack surface?
Staff who can be tricked by a phishing call
An open TCP port on a web server
An unlocked server room door
An outdated library in an application
Social engineering targets people. Open ports are digital; unlocked doors are physical.
d
Attack surface reduction
Which action most directly reduces the digital attack surface?
Removing unused internet-facing services
Buying a larger firewall appliance
Hiring more SOC analysts
Increasing log retention
Removing what is not needed eliminates exposure. Other measures improve detection or capacity but leave the surface unchanged.
d
Shadow IT
A forgotten test server with an old admin panel is found on the internet. Why is this a serious risk?
Unmanaged assets are often unpatched and unmonitored
Test servers cannot be scanned by attackers
Admin panels are always protected by default
Forgotten servers stop working after a year
Shadow and forgotten assets widen the attack surface and are frequent breach entry points.
m
Security, privacy, safety
How does privacy differ from security?
Privacy concerns appropriate use of personal data; security protects systems and data from threats
Privacy concerns only encryption; security concerns only passwords
Privacy applies to companies; security applies only to individuals
Privacy and security are two names for the same discipline
Strong security is needed for privacy, but a secure system can still use personal data inappropriately.
d
Safety
In an industrial plant, why can a safety system's priority conflict with a security control?
Safety may require systems to act or fail open immediately, even when security would lock them down
Safety systems are never connected to any network, so security does not apply
Security controls only apply to office IT, never to plants
Safety and security are always handled by the same tool
In cyber-physical systems, protecting human life can override confidentiality or access controls.
m
Threat actors
Which threat actor is typically motivated by financial gain?
Cybercriminal groups
Hacktivists
Nation-state espionage units
Curious script kiddies
Cybercriminals seek money through ransomware, fraud and data theft; hacktivists are ideologically motivated.
d
Threat actors
What typically distinguishes a nation-state actor from a criminal group?
Strategic goals, significant resources and long-term persistence
A preference for loud, quick attacks that demand ransom
Reliance only on freely available, unmodified tools
Targeting only home users rather than organisations
State actors pursue espionage or disruption with patience and resources, though tactics increasingly overlap with crime.
m
Insiders
Why are insider threats hard to detect?
Insiders already have legitimate access
Insiders never leave any logs or traces
Insiders use only physical attacks
Insiders always work with nation-states
Malicious or careless insiders act within authorised access, so detection relies on behavioural anomalies.
m
Terminology
Which statement correctly relates threat, vulnerability and risk?
Risk arises when a threat can exploit a vulnerability to harm an asset
A vulnerability is an attacker, and a threat is a software flaw
Risk exists only after an attack has already succeeded
A threat and a vulnerability are the same thing
A vulnerability is a weakness, a threat is something that could exploit it, and risk combines likelihood and impact.
d
Terminology
What is the difference between an exploit and a vulnerability?
A vulnerability is the weakness; an exploit is code or a technique that uses it
An exploit is the weakness; a vulnerability is the attacker's tool
Both terms describe the patch released by a vendor
A vulnerability exists only after an exploit is published
Weaknesses may exist for years before anyone writes an exploit, which is why patching does not wait for exploits.
d
Terminology
What is a false positive in security monitoring?
An alert raised for activity that is actually benign
A real attack that the monitoring system missed
A correct alert about genuine malicious activity
A log entry that has been deleted by an attacker
False positives waste analyst time; false negatives are missed attacks, which are usually more dangerous.
m
Terminology
What is an indicator of compromise (IoC)?
An observable artefact, such as a hash or IP address, linked to malicious activity
A policy document describing how to respond to incidents
A certificate showing a system has passed an audit
A tool that automatically patches vulnerable servers
IoCs such as file hashes, domains and IPs help detect known threats; behavioural indicators help with unknown ones.
